p.src: Now Liu Boqin and Tang Sanzang were still in a state of alarm when they again heard the cry, “Master, you have come!” The servants said, “That must be the old ape shut in the stone coffer at the foot of the mountain.” The Guardian said, “It is he, it is he.” Sanzang asked, “What old ape is that?” The Guardian replied, “This mountain was formerly called the Mountain of the Five Elements, but after our Great Tang king campaigned in the west and secured the realm, it was renamed the Mountain of Two Frontiers. Years ago, I heard the elders say that when Wang Mang usurped the Han throne, this mountain descended from Heaven and pinned beneath it a divine monkey. Neither cold nor heat troubled him, and he took no ordinary food or drink. An earth god was appointed to guard him and made him eat iron pellets when hungry and drink molten copper when thirsty. From that time to this, neither freezing nor starvation has killed him. The one calling out must certainly be he. Do not be afraid, Elder. Let us go down the mountain and see.” Sanzang could only consent, and led his horse down the mountain. After traveling only a few li, they saw that there really was a monkey between the rocks, with his head exposed and one hand stretched out. Waving frantically, he cried, “Master, why have you taken until now to come? How good that you have come! How good! Free me, and I shall protect you on your journey to the Western Heaven.” The Elder went closer and examined him carefully. What do you suppose he looked like?

p.src: Guardian Liu was truly bold. He stepped forward, pulled away the grass beside the monkey’s temples and the sedge beneath his chin, and asked, “What have you to say?” The monkey said, “I have nothing to say to you. Have that master come here, and I will ask him something.” Sanzang said, “What would you ask me?” The monkey asked, “Are you the one sent by the sovereign of the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven?” Sanzang replied, “I am indeed. Why do you ask?” The monkey said, “I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven who five hundred years ago caused havoc in the Celestial Palace. For the crime of defying my superiors with deceit, I was pinned here by the Buddha. Some time ago, the Bodhisattva Guanyin came by, bearing the Buddha’s decree and journeying to the Eastern Land to find a scripture pilgrim. I asked her to rescue me. She exhorted me never again to do violence, but to take refuge in the Buddha’s Law, devotedly protect the scripture pilgrim, and journey west to worship the Buddha; once my service was complete, I would receive my reward. Ever since, I have waited anxiously day and night, fearful from dawn to dusk, expecting only the Master to come and release me. I am willing to protect you as you fetch the scriptures and to become your disciple.” When Sanzang heard this, his heart filled with joy. “Though you possess this good intention, have received the Bodhisattva’s instruction, and wish to enter the Buddhist order, I have neither axe nor chisel. How can I free you?” The monkey said, “You need no axe or chisel. If only you are willing to save me, I can come out by myself.” Sanzang asked, “I will save you, but how can you get out?” The monkey replied, “At the summit of this mountain is a golden-lettered seal placed by our Buddha, the Tathagata. You need only climb the mountain and remove it, and I shall come out.” Following these instructions, Sanzang turned and appealed to Liu Boqin: “Guardian, come with me up the mountain.” Boqin said, “How do we know whether this is true or false?” The monkey cried loudly, “It is true! I would never dare deceive you.”

p.src: Boqin had no choice but to summon his servants and have them lead the horse. He himself supported Sanzang as they climbed the lofty mountain once more. Clinging to vines and creepers, they reached the very summit. Sure enough, they saw ten thousand shafts of golden light and a thousand streams of auspicious vapor. There stood a great square rock, upon which was affixed a seal bearing the six golden characters “Om mani padme hum.” Sanzang went forward and knelt. Facing the rock and gazing upon the golden characters, he bowed several times, then looked westward and prayed: “I, your disciple Chen Xuanzang, have received an imperial decree to seek the scriptures. If this monkey is destined to become my disciple, let me remove the golden-lettered seal and free the divine monkey, so that together we may attain enlightenment at Vulture Peak. But if no such bond exists, and this creature is a fierce and stubborn monster deceiving me so that no blessing may result, then let the seal prove impossible to remove.” When he had finished praying, he bowed again. After bowing, he stepped forward and gently peeled away the six golden characters. At once a fragrant wind arose, snatched the seal from his hand, and swept it into the sky, while a voice cried, “We are the guardians appointed to keep the Great Sage imprisoned. Today his term of tribulation is fulfilled. We shall return to the Tathagata and surrender this seal.” Sanzang, Boqin, and all their company were so startled that they bowed toward the sky. They went straight down the high mountain and returned to the stone coffer. Addressing the monkey, they said, “We have removed the seal. Come out now.” The monkey was delighted and cried, “Master, please move farther away so that I may come out. I would not have you frightened.”

p.src: Hearing this, Boqin led Sanzang and the others eastward at once. When they had gone some five or seven li, they again heard the monkey cry loudly, “Go farther! Farther still!” Sanzang and the others went a good deal farther and descended the mountain. Then they heard a tremendous crash, as though the earth had split and the mountain collapsed. Everyone trembled with fear. Suddenly they saw that the monkey had already reached Sanzang’s horse. Naked and dripping, he knelt and said, “Master, I am free!” He bowed four times to Sanzang, sprang to his feet, and made a deep salute to Boqin. “Many thanks, elder brother, for escorting my master, and for pulling the grass from my face.” After thanking him, the monkey went to arrange the baggage and fasten it upon the horse’s back. At the sight of him, the horse’s back weakened and its hooves faltered; trembling violently, it could scarcely remain standing. This was because the monkey had once been the Protector of Horses, charged in Heaven with tending the dragon steeds. He therefore possessed a certain authority over horses, and ordinary steeds were afraid when they saw him.

p.src: Sanzang saw from his manner that he truly had a good heart and indeed seemed fit for the Buddhist order. So he called, “Disciple, what is your surname?” The Monkey King replied, “My surname is Sun.” Sanzang said, “I shall give you a religious name, so that I may address you properly.” The Monkey King said, “There is no need to trouble yourself, Master. I already have a religious name: Sun Wukong.” Sanzang said with delight, “That accords perfectly with our school. With that appearance of yours, you look rather like a young mendicant. How would it be if I gave you the familiar title Pilgrim?” Wukong replied, “Good, good, good!” From that time onward, he was also known as Sun the Pilgrim.

p.src: When Boqin saw that Sun the Pilgrim was intent on preparing to depart, he turned, saluted Sanzang, and said, “Elder, I am most delighted that you have had the good fortune to acquire such a fine disciple here. He is certainly capable of making the journey. I must now take my leave and return home.” Sanzang bowed in gratitude and said, “I have greatly troubled you to accompany me and cannot express the depth of my thanks. When you return home, please convey my warmest respects to your honored mother and your wife. This poor monk imposed greatly upon your household; if I return, I shall visit again to offer my thanks in person.” Boqin returned the salute, and there the two parties took their separate ways.

p.src: Now Sun the Traveler asked Tripitaka to mount his horse, while he went ahead carrying the luggage, stark naked and striding along. Before long they had crossed Two Frontiers Mountain, when suddenly a fierce tiger came roaring toward them, lashing its tail. Tripitaka was terrified in the saddle. The Traveler rejoiced by the roadside and said, “Master, do not fear it. It has come to bring me some clothes.” He set down the luggage, pulled a needle from his ear, and waved it into the wind; it proved to be an iron staff as thick as a bowl. Taking it in his hand, he laughed and said, “I have not used this treasure for more than five hundred years. Today I shall bring it out and win myself something to wear.” Watch as he strode forward to meet the fierce tiger and cried, “You accursed beast! Where do you think you are going?” The tiger crouched down in the dust and did not dare move a muscle. He struck it squarely on the head with his staff, splattering its brains like ten thousand crimson peach blossoms and scattering its teeth like beads of jade. Chen Xuanzang was so frightened that he tumbled from the saddle, bit his finger, and exclaimed, “Heavens! Heavens! When Captain Liu fought that striped tiger the other day, he still had to battle it for half a day; yet today Sun Wukong needed no struggle at all and smashed this tiger to pulp with a single blow. Truly, however strong one may be, there is always someone stronger!”

p.src: The Traveler dragged the tiger over and said, “Master, sit for a moment while I strip off its clothes and put them on for the journey.” Tripitaka said, “What clothes could it possibly have?” The Traveler replied, “Never mind me, Master. I have my own way of doing it.” The fine Monkey King plucked out one of his hairs, breathed immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It changed into a sharp ox-ear knife. He slit open the skin at the tiger’s belly and peeled downward, removing the hide whole. He chopped off the claws, cut away the head, and fashioned a neat square of tiger skin. Lifting it up and measuring it, he said, “It is a little too broad. One piece will make two.” He took up the knife again and cut it into two pieces. He put one away and wrapped the other around his waist. He pulled up a kudzu vine by the roadside, bound it tightly around himself to cover his lower body, and said, “Master, let us be on our way. When we reach a house, we can borrow needle and thread and sew it then.” He gave the iron staff a twist, whereupon it became a needle again, and stored it in his ear. Then he shouldered the luggage and asked his master to mount the horse.

p.src: As the two continued onward, the elder asked from horseback, “Wukong, what became of the iron staff with which you struck the tiger just now?” The Traveler laughed and said, “Master, you do not know. I obtained this staff from the Dragon Palace in the Eastern Ocean. It is called the Divine Iron That Anchored the Bottom of the Milky Way, and also the Compliant Golden-Hooped Staff. It was of immense help to me when I rebelled against the Celestial Palace. It changes as I wish: when I want it large, it grows large; when I want it small, it grows small. Just now I changed it into the likeness of an embroidery needle and stored it inside my ear. I take it out only when I need it.” Tripitaka was secretly delighted to hear this. He asked again, “Why did that tiger remain perfectly still when it saw you just now? Why did it simply let you strike it at your leisure?” Wukong replied, “To tell you the truth, Master, let alone a tiger—even a dragon would not dare behave insolently before me. I, old Sun, possess the skill to subdue dragons and tame tigers, and the divine power to overturn rivers and churn the seas; I discern character from appearance and fathom meaning from the sound of a voice; grown large, I can fill the universe; grown small, I can be contained within a single hair; my transformations are limitless, and neither my concealment nor my appearance can be fathomed. What is so remarkable about skinning this tiger? When we come to some truly difficult place, then you shall see me display my abilities.” Hearing these words, Tripitaka felt more at ease than ever, cast off all anxiety, and urged his horse onward.

p.src: The Traveler said, “Master, quicken your pace a little; it is growing late. The trees are thick and dark over there, so there must be a household or manor nearby. Let us hurry there and seek lodging while there is still time.” Tripitaka duly urged his horse forward, made straight for the dwelling, and dismounted before the manor gate. The Traveler dropped the luggage, stepped forward, and shouted, “Open the gate! Open the gate!” An old man inside came out leaning on a bamboo staff and flung the gate open with a clatter. When he saw the Traveler’s ferocious countenance, with a tiger skin tied around his waist and a likeness like the Duke of Thunder, his legs went weak and his body numb with terror, and he babbled, “A demon has come! A demon has come!” Tripitaka stepped forward to support him and said, “Good elder, do not be afraid. He is this poor monk’s disciple, not a demon or monster.” The old man raised his head and, seeing Tripitaka’s refined and uncommon features, finally steadied himself and asked, “From what monastery do you monks come, that you bring this villain to my gate?” Tripitaka replied, “This poor monk comes from the Tang realm and is journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. We happened to pass this way, and as night has fallen, we have come especially to your honorable residence to borrow lodging for one night. We shall depart tomorrow before first light. I earnestly beg you to grant us this favor.” The old man said, “Though you may be a man of Tang, that vicious fellow is certainly no Tang man.” Wukong shouted sternly, “You old man have no discernment at all! The Tang man is my master, and I am his disciple. Nor am I any sugar man or honey man—I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven! There are people in this region who know me. I have seen you before as well.” The old man asked, “Where did you see me?” Wukong replied, “When you were young, did you not gather firewood before my face? Did you not pick vegetables upon my face?” The old man said, “This rogue speaks nonsense! Where did you live? Where did I live? How could I have gathered firewood and picked vegetables before you?” Wukong said, “May my son be the one speaking nonsense! You simply fail to recognize me. I am the Great Sage who lived in the stone casket beneath Two Frontiers Mountain. Take another good look.” Only then did the old man understand, and he said, “You do look somewhat like him. But how did you manage to get out?” Wukong related to the old man in detail how the Bodhisattva had exhorted him to reform, instructed him to await the Tang monk, and arranged for the seal to be removed so that he might be freed.

p.src: Only then did the old man bow, invite the Tang monk inside, and call his aged wife and children to meet them. When he told them all that had happened before, every one of them rejoiced. He also ordered tea to be served. When they had finished their tea, he asked Wukong, “Great Sage, you too must be advanced in years?” Wukong replied, “How old are you this year?” The old man said, “Unworthy though I am, I have reached the age of one hundred and thirty.” The Traveler said, “Why, you are still one of my great-great-grandsons. I do not remember when I myself was born; but I have been at the foot of this mountain alone for more than five hundred years.” The old man said, “Indeed, indeed. I remember my grandfather saying that this mountain descended from Heaven and pinned a divine monkey beneath it. Only now have you finally escaped. When I saw you as a child, you had grass on your head and mud on your face, so I was not afraid of you; but now the mud is gone from your face and the grass from your head, you seem rather thinner, and you have that great tiger skin wrapped around your waist—how different do you look from a demon?” When the whole family heard him speak this way, they all burst into hearty laughter.

When I saw you as a child, you had grass on your head and mud on your face, so I was not afraid of you;
but now the mud is gone from your face and the grass from your head, you seem rather thinner, and you have that great tiger skin wrapped around your waist—how different do you look from a demon?”
When the whole family heard him speak this way, they all burst into hearty laughter.

p.src: The old man was a most worthy fellow and at once ordered a vegetarian meal to be prepared. After the meal, Wukong asked, “What is your family name?” The old man replied, “Our family name is Chen.” Hearing this, Tripitaka immediately dismounted, raised his joined hands, and said, “Venerable benefactor, you and this poor monk are of the same clan.” The Pilgrim said, “Master, your surname is Tang. How can you be of the same clan as he?” Tripitaka said, “My lay family name is also Chen. I come from Juxian Village in Hongnong Commandery, Haizhou, in the Great Tang. My Dharma name is Chen Xuanzang. It was only because Emperor Taizong of our Great Tang made me his imperial younger brother and named me Tripitaka, assigning Tang as my surname, that I came to be called the Tang Monk.” When the old man heard that they shared a surname, he was more delighted than ever.

p.src: The Pilgrim said, “Old Chen, since we are already troubling your household, there is one more thing. I have not bathed in over five hundred years. Would you heat some water so that my master and I may wash? Then, before we leave, we shall have troubled you thoroughly.” The old man immediately had water heated and basins brought out, and lamps were lit. When master and disciple had finished bathing, they sat before the lamp. The Pilgrim said, “Old Chen, there is one more thing I must trouble you for: lend me a needle and thread.” The old man replied, “Yes, yes, certainly.” He had his wife fetch a needle and thread and hand them to the Pilgrim. The Pilgrim was quick-witted. Seeing that his master had taken off a short white cotton robe to bathe and had not yet put it back on, he snatched it up and draped it over himself. Then he took off the tiger skin and stitched its edges together. He pleated it like a horse-face skirt, wrapped it around his waist, and fastened it with a strip of rattan. Then he went before his master and said, “How does Old Sun’s attire today compare with yesterday’s?” Tripitaka said, “Good, good, good. Dressed like that, you finally look like a true pilgrim.” Tripitaka added, “Disciple, if you do not mind that robe being worn and old, you may keep it and wear it.” Wukong bowed and said, “Many thanks for the gift, many thanks.” He then found some fodder and fed the horse. By then all their tasks were done, and the master and disciple and the old man each retired for the night.

p.src: After master and disciple had travelled for some time, a sudden whistle sounded beside the road, and six men burst forth, each armed with long spears, short swords, keen blades, or powerful bows. They roared, “Where do you think you’re going, monk? Leave your horse and baggage at once, and we’ll spare your life and let you pass.” Tripitaka was so terrified that his soul nearly left his body. He tumbled from the horse and could not utter a word. The Pilgrim helped him up and said, “Do not worry, Master. It is nothing at all. These men have come to give us clothes and travelling money.” Tripitaka said, “Wukong, you must be a little hard of hearing. They told us to leave our horse and luggage, yet you say you will ask them for clothes and travelling money.” The Pilgrim said, “You just guard the clothes, luggage, and horse. Let Old Sun contend with them awhile and see what comes of it.” Tripitaka said, “Even a good fighter cannot withstand two fists, and two fists are no match for four hands. There are six great hulking men over there, while you are such a little fellow. How dare you contend with them?”

p.src: The Pilgrim was bold by nature and would hear no argument. He strode forward, clasped his hands before his chest, bowed to the six men, and said, “Gentlemen, why are you blocking this poor monk’s way?” One of the men said, “We are great kings who waylay travellers and benevolent lords of the mountain. Our great names have long been renowned, though naturally you know nothing of them. Leave your possessions at once, and we shall let you pass; but if you utter so much as half a ‘no,’ we shall smash your corpse and grind your bones to powder.” The Pilgrim said, “I too am a hereditary great king and a mountain lord of many years, yet I have never heard of any great names belonging to you gentlemen.” The man said, “You do not know, so I shall tell you. One is called Eye-Seeing-Joy, another Ear-Hearing-Anger, another Nose-Smelling-Love, another Tongue-Tasting-Thought, another Mind-Conceiving-Desire, and another Body-Rooted-Sorrow.” Wukong laughed and said, “So you are merely six petty thieves. You fail to recognize that this monk is your true master, and instead you come to block my road. Bring out the treasures you have plundered. I shall divide them with you, seven parts to me, and then I may spare you.” At these words, the thieves reacted each according to his nature—the joyous one rejoiced, the angry one raged, the loving one loved, the thoughtful one brooded, the desirous one desired, and the sorrowful one grieved. They all surged forward, shouting wildly, “What an insolent monk! You have not a single possession of your own, yet you turn around and demand a share of ours!” Brandishing spears and flourishing swords, they rushed him in a mass and hacked wildly at the Pilgrim’s head. Clang and crash—they struck him seventy or eighty times. Wukong stood still in their midst as though he noticed nothing. One of the thieves said, “What a monk! His head truly is hard.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “It is tolerable enough. Your hands must be weary from striking me. Now it is Old Sun’s turn to take out a little needle and have some fun.” One thief said, “This monk must be a physician who practises acupuncture in disguise. None of us is ill, so why are you talking about using a needle?”

p.src: The Pilgrim reached into his ear and pulled out an embroidery needle. With one flourish in the wind, it became an iron staff as thick as a rice bowl. Taking it in hand, he cried, “Do not run! Let Old Sun try his hand with a stroke of the staff.” The six robbers were so terrified that they scattered in every direction. But he lengthened his stride and chased them down one after another, circling about until he had beaten every one of them to death. He stripped off their clothes, seized their traveling money, and came back smiling. “Master, let us be on our way. Old Sun has wiped out the robbers.” Tripitaka said, “You have brought terrible trouble upon us. Highwaymen though they were, even if they had been taken before the magistrate, their crimes would not have deserved death. For all your powers, you should merely have driven them off. Why did you beat them all to death? This is the wanton taking of human life. How can you be a monk? Those who have left the world fear as they sweep that they may harm the ants, and shield their lamps with gauze out of pity for the moths. How could you make no distinction between right and wrong and beat them all dead in one onslaught? You have not the least compassion or love of goodness. It is only fortunate that here in the wilderness there is no one to investigate. If we reach a town and someone happens to offend you, will you turn violent again, brandish your staff, and indiscriminately injure people? I could hardly remain an innocent bystander—how could I escape implication?” Wukong said, “Master, if I had not killed them, they would have killed you.” Tripitaka said, “As one who has left the world, I would rather die than dare to commit violence. If I died, only one life would be lost; but you have killed six men. How could that be justified? If this affair were reported to the authorities, even if your own father were the magistrate, he could not argue your way out of it.” The Pilgrim said, “I will not hide it from you, Master. Five hundred years ago, when Old Sun occupied the Mountain of Flowers and Fruit, proclaimed himself king, and lived as a monster, I cannot say how many people I killed. If, as you say, every such deed had been brought before the authorities and charges laid, I could never have become the ‘Great Sage Equal to Heaven.’” Tripitaka said, “It was precisely because you were subject to neither restraint nor rule, tyrannized the human world, defied Heaven, and deceived your superiors that the calamity of five hundred years ago befell you. Now that you have entered the Buddhist fold, if you still commit violence as before and persist in taking life, you will never reach the Western Heaven and can never be a monk. Utterly wicked! Utterly wicked!”

p.src: Now this monkey had never in his life been able to endure another’s reproach. When he saw Tripitaka nagging on and on, he could no longer suppress the fire in his heart and burst out, “Since that is how you feel, and you say I cannot be a monk or reach the Western Heaven, you need not keep babbling and vexing me. I shall simply go back.” Tripitaka made no reply. In a fit of temper, the monkey sprang into the air and cried, “Old Sun is off!” Tripitaka hastily looked up, but he had already vanished. He heard only a whoosh as Wukong sped back east. Left entirely alone, the elder shook his head, sighed to himself, and lamented bitterly, “That wretch is so unwilling to accept instruction! I merely said a few words to him, yet how could he disappear without a trace and head straight back? Enough, enough, enough! It must be my fate not to take a disciple or add another mouth to my household. Now there is nowhere to seek him, and if I call, he will not answer. Onward, then! Onward!” Indeed: Give up the body, stake your life, and journey west; rely on no one else, but decide your course yourself.

p.src: The elder had no choice but to gather his luggage and strap it to the horse. He did not mount, but walked on westward in desolation, holding his priest’s staff in one hand and the reins in the other. Before he had gone far, he saw an aged woman on the mountain road ahead, carrying a padded garment with a flowered cap resting upon it. When Tripitaka saw her draw near, he hastily led his horse to the right side of the road and stood aside to let her pass. The old woman asked, “From where do you come, Reverend, that you travel here all alone and forlorn?” Tripitaka replied, “This disciple was sent from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to worship the living Buddha in the Western Heaven and seek the true scriptures.” The old woman said, “The Buddha of the West dwells at the Great Thunderclap Monastery within the borders of India. It is a journey of one hundred and eight thousand li from here. You have only one man and one horse, with neither companion nor disciple. How can you possibly get there?” Tripitaka said, “A few days ago, this disciple took on an apprentice, but he was wild, fierce, and unruly. When I admonished him with a few words, he refused instruction and vanished.” The old woman said, “I have here a cotton monk’s robe and a flowered cap inlaid with gold. They belonged to my son, who became a monk for only three days before his short life ended in misfortune. I have just been to his monastery to weep, bid farewell to his master, and bring away these two articles, robe and cap, as keepsakes. Reverend, since you have a disciple, let me give you this robe and cap.” Tripitaka said, “I am deeply grateful for your generous gift, good mother, but my disciple has already left, so I dare not accept it.” The old woman asked, “Which way did he go?” Tripitaka replied, “I heard a whoosh, and he went back east.” The old woman said, “My home lies not far to the east. He must have gone there. At home I also have a spell called the ‘True Words for Calming the Mind,’ otherwise known as the ‘Headband-Tightening Spell.’ Learn it secretly by heart, fix it firmly in your mind, and never divulge it to anyone. I shall catch up with him and tell him to return and follow you; then you must have him put on this robe and cap. If he refuses to obey your commands, silently recite the spell. Then he will never again dare to commit violence or run away.” Hearing this, Tripitaka bowed his head and thanked her. The old woman transformed into a beam of golden light and flew back east. Tripitaka knew at once that Guanyin Bodhisattva had bestowed this true formula upon him. He hurriedly scooped up earth for an incense burner, burned incense, and bowed fervently toward the east. When he had finished bowing, he took the robe and cap and hid them inside his bundle. He then sat beside the road and practiced the True Words for Calming the Mind, reciting them back and forth several times until he knew them perfectly and had fixed them firmly in his heart. Of this, no more need be said.

p.src: Now Wukong, having left his master, turned a somersault cloud and headed straight back across the Eastern Ocean. He brought his cloud to a halt, parted the waters, and went directly to the Crystal Palace. The Dragon King was promptly alerted and came out to welcome him, escorting him into the palace and seating him there. When the courtesies were concluded, the Dragon King said, “I recently heard that the Great Sage had completed his term of suffering. Forgive me for failing to offer my congratulations! I suppose you intend to restore your immortal mountain and return to your ancient cave?” Wukong replied, “I was so inclined, but I have become a monk again.” The Dragon King asked, “What sort of monk?” The Pilgrim said, “Thanks to the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea, who urged me toward goodness and taught me to seek the true fruit, I began following a Tang monk from the Eastern Land westward to worship the Buddha. I entered the Buddhist fold and am now also called the Pilgrim.” The Dragon King said, “Then this is truly cause for congratulations—congratulations indeed. This is what it truly means to forsake evil and return to righteousness, to learn from punishment and awaken a good heart. If that is so, why are you not traveling west? Why have you returned east?” The Pilgrim laughed. “That Tang monk has no understanding of a man’s nature. A few petty robbers barred the road, so I beat them to death. The Tang monk then nagged endlessly and found all manner of fault with me. Do you imagine Old Sun is one to swallow such resentment in silence? So I left him and decided to return to my own mountain. I came first to pay you a visit and ask for a cup of tea.” The Dragon King said, “We are honored by your visit, deeply honored.” At once, the Dragon King’s sons and grandsons brought fragrant tea and presented it to him.

p.src: When they had finished their tea, the Traveler turned and saw a painting of “Presenting the Shoe at the Yi Bridge” hanging on the rear wall. “What scene is this?” asked the Traveler. The Dragon King replied, “This happened after your time, Great Sage, so you do not recognize it. It is called ‘Presenting the Shoe Three Times at the Yi Bridge.’” “Why ‘presenting the shoe three times’?” asked the Traveler. The Dragon King said, “This immortal is the Yellow-Stone Elder, and this young man is Zhang Liang of the Han dynasty. While the Elder sat upon the Yi Bridge, he suddenly dropped his shoe beneath it and called on Zhang Liang to retrieve it. The young man hurried to fetch it, then knelt and offered it to him. This happened three times, yet Zhang Liang showed not the slightest arrogance or impatience. Admiring his diligence and respect, the Elder taught him a heavenly book by night and charged him to support the Han. Later, as expected, he devised strategies within the command tent that decided victories a thousand leagues away. Once peace was restored, he relinquished his office and retired to the mountains, where he roamed with Master Red Pine and attained the Way of Immortality. Great Sage, if you will not protect the Tang Monk, labor diligently, and accept instruction, you will remain a mere monster-immortal and can forget about attaining the true fruit.” Hearing this, Wukong pondered in silence for a long while. The Dragon King said, “You must decide for yourself, Great Sage. Do not seek only your own ease and ruin your future.” Wukong said, “Enough talk. Old Sun will go back and protect him.” The Dragon King said joyfully, “In that case, I dare not detain you. Please show mercy at once, Great Sage, and do not leave your master unattended too long.”

u.src: When they had finished their tea, the Traveler turned and saw a painting of “Presenting the Shoe at the Yi Bridge” hanging on the rear wall.
“What scene is this?” asked the Traveler.
The Dragon King replied, “This happened after your time, Great Sage, so you do not recognize it.
It is called ‘Presenting the Shoe Three Times at the Yi Bridge.’”
“Why ‘presenting the shoe three times’?” asked the Traveler.

The Dragon King said, “This immortal is the Yellow-Stone Elder, and this young man is Zhang Liang of the Han dynasty. While the Elder sat upon the Yi Bridge, he suddenly dropped his shoe beneath it and called on Zhang Liang to retrieve it.
The young man hurried to fetch it, then knelt and offered it to him.

This happened three times, yet Zhang Liang showed not the slightest arrogance or impatience. Admiring his diligence and respect, the Elder taught him a heavenly book by night and charged him to support the Han.
Later, as expected, he devised strategies within the command tent that decided victories a thousand leagues away.
Once peace was restored, he relinquished his office and retired to the mountains, where he roamed with Master Red Pine and attained the Way of Immortality.
Great Sage, if you will not protect the Tang Monk, labor diligently, and accept instruction, you will remain a mere monster-immortal and can forget about attaining the true fruit.”
Hearing this, Wukong pondered in silence for a long while.
The Dragon King said, “You must decide for yourself, Great Sage. Do not seek only your own ease and ruin your future.”
Wukong said, “Enough talk. Old Sun will go back and protect him.”
The Dragon King said joyfully, “In that case, I dare not detain you. Please show mercy at once, Great Sage, and do not leave your master unattended too long.”

p.src: Seeing that the Dragon King was urging him to depart, the Traveler sprang up, left the ocean treasury, mounted a cloud, and took his leave. As he traveled, he encountered the Bodhisattva of the Southern Sea. The Bodhisattva said, “Sun Wukong, why have you refused instruction and abandoned the Tang Monk? What brings you here?” Alarmed, the Traveler saluted her from his cloud and said, “Thanks to the Bodhisattva’s kind words before, a monk of the Tang indeed arrived, removed the seal that held me down, and saved my life, so I became his disciple. But he reproached me for being fierce and unruly, so I slipped away from him for a moment. I am going back to protect him now.” The Bodhisattva said, “Go quickly, before you lose your resolve.” With that, each went their own way.

p.src: In a moment, the Traveler saw the Tang Monk sitting dejectedly by the roadside. He went up and said, “Master, why are you not traveling on? What are you still doing here?” Tripitaka looked up and said, “Where have you been? I dared neither go on nor make a move without you, and could only wait here for your return.” The Traveler said, “I went to the old Dragon King’s palace in the Eastern Ocean for some tea.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, one who has left the household must not lie. You have been away from me for less than an hour, yet you claim to have visited the Dragon King for tea?” The Traveler laughed. “To tell you the truth, Master, I can ride the Somersault Cloud. A single somersault carries me one hundred and eight thousand li, so I can go and return at once.” Tripitaka said, “My words were only a little harsh, yet you took offense, lost your temper, and abandoned me. With your abilities, you can find tea to drink; but one like me, who cannot travel as you do, can only sit here and endure hunger. How could you have the heart?” The Traveler said, “Master, if you are hungry, I will go beg some vegetarian food for you.” Tripitaka said, “There is no need to beg for food. Some provisions that Commandant Liu’s mother gave us are still in my bundle. Take the bowl and find some water, so that I may eat a little before we set off.”

p.src: The Traveler untied the bundle and found several coarse-flour flatbreads inside. He took them out and handed them to his master. He also saw a gleaming cotton robe and a flowered cap inlaid with gold. The Traveler asked, “Did you bring these clothes and this cap from the Eastern Land?” Tripitaka readily replied, “I wore them when I was young. If you put on this cap, you will know how to recite scriptures without being taught; and if you put on this robe, you will know how to perform the rites without instruction.” The Traveler said, “Good Master, let me put them on.” Tripitaka said, “I fear they may not fit you, but if they do, you may wear them.” The Traveler took off his old white-cloth robe and put on the cotton one. It fitted him as though it had been cut to his measure. Then he put on the cap. When Tripitaka saw that the cap was on his head, he left his provisions untouched and silently recited the Tight-Fillet Spell once. The Traveler cried, “My head hurts! My head hurts!” His master recited it several more times without pause, and the pain sent the Traveler rolling on the ground until he tore apart the gold-inlaid flowered cap. Fearing that he might break the golden fillet as well, Tripitaka stopped reciting. As soon as he stopped, the pain ceased. The Traveler reached up and felt his head. Something like a golden thread was gripping it tightly; he could neither remove nor break it, for it had already taken root there. He took the needle from his ear, inserted it beneath the fillet, and pried wildly outward. Fearing that he would pry it apart, Tripitaka began reciting again. The pain returned as before. He stood on his head and turned somersaults, his ears red, his face flushed, his eyes bulging, and his whole body numb. Seeing him in such a state, his master could not bear it and once more fell silent. The pain in his head ceased again. The Traveler said, “So it was you, Master, who cursed my head?” Tripitaka said, “I was reciting the Tight-Fillet Scripture. When did I ever curse you?” The Traveler said, “Recite it again and let us see.” Tripitaka really did recite it again. The Traveler truly felt the pain again and cried, “Do not recite it! Do not recite it! The moment you recite it, I feel pain. What is the meaning of this?” Tripitaka said, “Will you heed my instruction now?” The Traveler replied, “I will heed it.” “And will you behave insolently again?” The Traveler said, “I would not dare.”

p.src: Though he agreed aloud, evil intent still lurked in his heart. He shook the needle until it became as thick as a bowl and was about to strike the Tang Monk. In alarm, the elder recited the spell two or three more times. The monkey fell to the ground, dropped his iron staff, and could not even raise a hand. He could only cry, “Master, I understand now! Do not recite it again! Do not recite it again!” Tripitaka said, “How could you betray your conscience and dare to strike me?” The Traveler said, “I never dared strike you. Let me ask you, Master: who taught you this spell?” Tripitaka replied, “An old woman I met just now taught it to me.” The Traveler flew into a rage. “Say no more! That old woman was surely Guanyin. How could she harm me so? I will go to the Southern Sea and beat her!” Tripitaka said, “Since she taught me this spell, she must already know it herself. If you seek her out and she begins reciting it, will you not die?” The Traveler saw the sense in this and truly dared not set out. He had no choice but to change his heart, kneel, and plead, “Master, this is her means of subduing me and making me follow you westward. I will not provoke her, but you must not treat the spell as an everyday saying and recite it whenever you please. I swear to protect you and will never again think of turning back.” Tripitaka said, “In that case, help me mount the horse.” Only then did the Traveler submit wholeheartedly. Rousing his spirits, he tightened his cotton robe, saddled the horse, gathered the luggage, and set off westward.
